minutes.headline: Chair refused a commissioner's PFAS/manganese cost-saving proposal presentation, deferring it to next meeting.
minutes.summary: The Water District Commissioners discussed IT/cybersecurity costs, adopted an informal policy requiring commissioners to give advance notice before adding substantive items to the agenda, and voted to put water-quality (PFAS/manganese) data on the district website. The bulk of the meeting was a heated dispute over whether a commissioner could present, that day, a proposal to avoid a roughly $40 million treatment plant by blending well water; the chair deferred it to the next meeting pending input from DEP, and the district also reported progress on the Metal Lane/Rolling Acres water main project.

public_comment.topic: Praised the new TV/display at the office and asked whether it could show something like a Patriots game; noted an upcoming presentation from a 'tank guy'.

votes.motion: Upload the manganese and PFAS data spreadsheet and corresponding charts to the district website, kept current, updated at minimum quarterly

budget_items.what_was_said: Commissioners discussed an IT/cybersecurity service contract, noting a grant covered roughly half of an annual fee. Different figures were given for various coverage tiers (full 24/7 coverage vs. monthly items like email hosting).

budget_items.topic: Website setup fee for water-quality data page
budget_items.what_was_said: The website vendor quoted a one-time fee to set up a page for water quality data, with no expected increase to the existing monthly maintenance fee.

budget_items.topic: PFAS/manganese treatment plant vs. alternative proposal
budget_items.what_was_said: A commissioner argued the standard treatment-plant solution for PFAS would cost roughly forty million dollars and urged the board to investigate a cheaper well-blending alternative to avoid that cost.
The same commissioner said the treatment-plant option would also carry an ongoing annual operating cost on top of the capital cost.

budget_items.topic: Potential savings from blending proposal vs. plant
budget_items.what_was_said: The commissioner said that if DEP approved his blending approach without a new plant, it would save water customers the plant's capital cost plus its annual operating expense.
The treasurer said the district would keep pursuing an additional cyber-related grant, with no figures given.

decisions.decision: The chair will have authority to add or remove agenda items; a commissioner wanting an item on the agenda must request it through the clerk/treasurer in advance so others can review it before the meeting it is discussed.
The $125 website setup fee will be covered as part of the existing website maintenance budget without a separate vote.

Commissioner Bill's PFAS/manganese well-blending proposal will not be presented at this meeting; he will send it by email for the other commissioners to review, and it will be discussed at the next meeting.

The board will wait for a meeting with DEP (expected around October, involving Lauren Thistle, Paula Karen, and Randy Swiger) before deciding whether well blending is a viable path, rather than evaluating the proposal beforehand.

what_happened.line: The chair declined to let a commissioner present his plan to blend well water instead of building a new treatment plant, deferring it to the next meeting pending state DEP input.
Commissioners voted to post the district's manganese and PFAS testing data and charts on its website, updated at least quarterly.
The board set an informal rule that a commissioner must request an agenda item through the clerk-treasurer in advance rather than raise it the day of a meeting.
A commissioner argued the standard PFAS/manganese treatment approach carries a large capital cost plus an ongoing annual operating cost, and said well-blending could avoid both if DEP approves it.

why_it_matters: Which treatment path the district picks for PFAS and manganese -- a new plant or well-blending -- will set the size of a capital project that ratepayers eventually finance through water rates.
Public posting of the water-quality data lets residents check manganese and PFAS levels themselves rather than take the board's word for it.
The new advance-notice rule for agenda items changes how a commissioner or resident gets a substantive proposal in front of the board on a given meeting date.
